questions.text: What exactly is in the emailed link, and who builds it? Is it the API server, or the worker, that turns the raw token into the URL?
How does the token get from the URL into a hidden field and out of the URL bar? Is that a redirect, or does the page script do it?
questions.about: CHOOSE NEW PASSWORD PAGE (token kept in a hidden field, stripped from the URL bar)

questions.text: Where does the breached-password list live? Is it a local file, a database table, or an external service?
questions.about: 2. pw >= 12 chars? not on breached list?

questions.text: For an unknown email, the document says to do nothing. How is the response time kept close to the known-email path? Is that a requirement or a suggestion?
The 'changed' email is enqueued after COMMIT. What does the user see if that enqueue fails? And does the 302 to /login still happen?
What does the worker do with the job payload on success, and what does 'delete the payload' mean for the queue you use? Who does it?
How is the email address matched to a user (case, whitespace)? What if two accounts could share an address?
Does a user with an unexpired link who then logs in normally and remembers their password still have a live reset link? Does anything cancel it?
questions.about: used_at null until the link is burned (used OR superseded)

answers.text: The API server builds the link (https://<app>/reset?token=<raw token>) and puts the finished link in the job; the worker only sends it. This keeps the worker unchanged and the token handling in one place.

No redirect. The server renders the page with the token in a hidden field, and the page script calls history.replaceState to remove it from the URL bar. Referrer-Policy: no-referrer stops it leaking in the meantime. Simplest option and it needs no extra round trip.
Not known where the breached-password list lives; the brief only calls it 'the breached-password list'. The design needs only a yes/no lookup and fails closed if it is down. Added to Open questions.
It is a recommendation, not a requirement; the brief only requires the same message and status. Suggested approach: do the DB work but don't wait for the enqueue. Note reworded to say so.
The failure is only logged. The password is already changed and committed, so the 302 to /login still happens. Failure-paths line now says so explicitly.

I do not know which queue technology is used or how it retains payloads. The design requirement is that no payload survives after send or drop, and that job bodies are not logged. Who enforces it (queue config or worker) needs confirming; added to Open questions.

Email is trimmed and lowercased before lookup (decided, stated in the diagram). Whether users.email is unique or stored lowercased is not known; the design assumes one user per normalised address. Added to Open questions.
Yes, the link stays live until it expires or is superseded; normal login does not cancel it. The brief does not require cancelling, and adding it would add a mechanism. One note line added.

questions.text: When the user clicks the emailed link, which token does the POST /reset use to look up the row, and what exactly does the 'Reset' form send back: the hidden-field T plus the new password only? Does the user need to be logged in or identified some other way?
On the Forgot-password page, after the user submits, what do they see and where does that response come from? Is the 200 body rendered as a page by the server, or shown by the browser script?
questions.about: 200 "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link."

questions.text: In the request flow, the SELECT user FOR UPDATE and the enqueue happen inside the transaction. What does 'enqueue' actually do: a write to the queue system (separate from Postgres) or an insert into a Postgres table? If the COMMIT fails after a successful enqueue, what happens to the job?
questions.about: enqueue job {to, link} ... COMMIT (if enqueue fails: ROLLBACK, old link survives, log)

questions.text: What is the 'worker' and how does it get triggered: does it poll the queue, or is it pushed jobs? Does it run as a separate process from the API server?
What does the 'changed' email contain and who is it sent to, and is the address taken from the users row for the user_id returned by the burn UPDATE?

Step 1 re-checks the token, then step 3 burns it. If the password is rejected in step 2 and the user retries, does each retry go through steps 1 to 3 again from scratch? And what does 'fail closed' on the breach-list lookup show the user exactly?
questions.about: 2. pw >= 12 chars? not on breached list?

questions.text: How does the API know which user's sessions to delete: from the user_id returned by the UPDATE ... RETURNING? And what happens to other pending reset links of that user (unused, unexpired) after a successful reset?

answers.text: The POST uses the hidden-field token T to look up the row via sha256(T). The form sends only T and the new password. No login is needed; the token is the credential. Stated beside the POST in the diagram.

The API returns the 200 with the generic body, and the client shows that body to the user. Whether the client is a script or a server-rendered page is a client detail the design does not need. Marked in the diagram as 'client shows the body'.

Enqueue is a write to the existing email queue, which is separate from Postgres (the brief says the API adds a job). Enqueue happens just before COMMIT. If COMMIT then fails, the job may still send, but its link has no row and shows the expired page. I accept this rare case and the user can re-request. Added to failure paths. What the queue is built on is not known.

The worker is the existing email worker from the brief, and I assume it is a separate process. I do not know whether it polls or is pushed jobs. The design does not depend on it. Added to Open questions.

Yes. The address is users.email of the user_id (U) returned by the burn UPDATE. The content is a short fixed 'your password was changed' notice; exact wording is not decided in this design. Added to step 4.

Yes. Each retry is a new POST that runs steps 1 to 3 from scratch, and only step 3 burns the token. When the breach-list lookup is down, the form is re-shown with a 'try again later' message and the link is not burned. Both are now in the diagram.

Yes. U is the user_id returned by UPDATE ... RETURNING. No other live link can exist, because issuing a new link already kills any earlier unused one, so at most one live link exists per user and the successful reset burns it. Noted in the DATA block.

teachbacks.text:
1. Setup. Postgres has one new table, password_reset_tokens. Each row has id, user_id, token_hash (the SHA-256 of the token; unique and indexed), created_at, expires_at (created_at + 30 min), and used_at. used_at is null until the link is "burned", which happens when it is either used or replaced by a newer link. Only the hash is stored. An index on (user_id, created_at) supports the rate-limit count. At most one live link per user exists at a time.

2. The user clicks "Forgot password?" and the browser sends POST /forgot with {email}. The API server trims and lowercases the email, then looks the user up in Postgres.

3. Unknown email. If no user matches, the server does nothing: no row, no job. It still returns the same response as every other branch (step 9).

4. Known user. The server opens a transaction (BEGIN) and runs SELECT user FOR UPDATE on that user's row. This makes concurrent requests for the same user run one after another.

5. Rate limit. Inside the transaction, the server counts that user's rows in password_reset_tokens with created_at in the last hour. If the count is 3 or more, it rolls back and creates no link and no job. The older link is untouched. The response is still the generic one.

6. Creating the link. If the count is under 3, the server:
   - sets used_at=now() on all of the user's rows where used_at is null, which kills any older link;
   - generates 32 random bytes as the token;
   - inserts a row holding sha256(token), the current time and now+30 min;
   - builds the link https://<app>/reset?token=<raw token>;
   - enqueues a job {to, link} on the email queue, which is separate from Postgres;
   - commits.
   If the enqueue fails, it rolls back, so the old link survives, and it logs the error. If COMMIT fails after a successful enqueue, the email may still go out, but its link will show the expired page. The document accepts this as rare.

7. Sending the email. A separate worker process takes the job from the queue and sends the email through the provider. On failure it retries 3 times with backoff. If it still fails, it logs and drops the job, and nobody is notified. The user gets no link, and the failed attempt still counts toward the 3-per-hour limit.

8. The raw token lives only in the emailed link, the queue job payload and the user's browser. Job bodies must not be logged.

9. Response. Every branch returns the same status and body: 200 "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." The client shows that body. This stops anyone from telling which emails have accounts. Similar response timing is only a recommendation.

10. The user clicks the emailed link, and the browser sends GET /reset?token=T. The server computes h = sha256(T) and runs a read-only SELECT for a row with token_hash=h, used_at null and expires_at in the future. GET burns nothing, so mail scanners and link previewers cannot use the link up.

11. If no row matches (unknown, expired, used or superseded), the server shows the EXPIRED PAGE: "This link has expired, request a new one".

12. If a row matches, the server shows the choose-new-password page. The response carries Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. The server puts T in a hidden form field, and the page script calls history.replaceState to remove the token from the URL bar.

13. The user submits, and the browser sends POST /reset with {T, pw}. The form sends only the hidden token and the new password. No login is needed, because the token is the credential. Every retry starts again at the step 13 checks.

14. Submit check 1. The server re-checks the token as in step 10. If it fails, the user sees the expired page.

15. Submit check 2. The server checks that the password is at least 12 characters and not on the breached list. If it fails, the form is shown again with the reason and the link stays usable until it expires. If the breach-list lookup is down, the server fails closed: the form is shown again with "try again later" and the link is not burned.

16. Submit step 3, the burn and password change. The server opens a transaction and runs a conditional UPDATE that sets used_at=now() WHERE token_hash=h AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now(), RETURNING user_id (U). If it returns 0 rows, because the user lost a race or the link just expired, the server rolls back and shows the expired page. This is how a double-submit or two tabs lets exactly one request win. Otherwise, in the same transaction, it sets users.password_hash=hash(pw) for U and deletes all of U's rows in sessions, then commits. Deleting the sessions logs out every device, including this one, because the API checks sessions on every request. If a DB error occurs, everything rolls back and the password, link and sessions are unchanged.

17. Submit step 4. After the commit, the server enqueues a short fixed "your password was changed" email to users.email of U. The same queue and worker as in step 7 handle it. If the enqueue fails or the mail is dropped, the failure is only logged. The password is already changed.

18. The server replies 302 to /login. No session is created, so the user must log in with the new password.

19. Other behaviours the document states. Two quick requests means only the newest link works. Logging in normally does not cancel an unexpired link. A nightly job can purge rows older than a day, and rows are not deleted within the hour so that the same table serves as the rate-limit counter.
gaps: Where the breached-password list lives (local file, table or service). The document says only that the check is a yes/no lookup.
Whether users.email is unique and stored lowercased. The document assumes one user per normalised address, so I cannot say what happens if two users match.
How the queue removes payloads after a job is sent or dropped. The document says this needs confirming with the queue owner.
How the password is hashed (the algorithm behind hash(pw)). The document does not say, and I did not need it to follow the flow.
